question:
Why are hydrogen, deuterium, and graphite used as neutron moderators in nuclear reactors, and what are typical neutron speed reductions after moderation?
(Context: preparing a lesson for Class 11 students in India (NCERT/CBSE) on "Work, Energy and Power". The point to support: The neutron moderation example gives the physics but lacks real reactor context: common moderators (light water, heavy water, graphite), why light nuclei are effective, and typical neutron speed/energy reductions.)
answer:
I have enough from authoritative sources (Wikipedia's neutron pages, the IAEA graphite knowledge base, and the World Nuclear Association). Here's a lesson-ready answer.

# Neutron moderation: physics + real reactor context

## 1. Why a moderator is needed at all

Uranium-235 fission releases neutrons that are **fast**: mean energy ≈ **2 MeV**, speed ≈ **20,000 km/s (2×10⁷ m/s)** (the spectrum is broad, mode ≈ 0.75 MeV, up to ~17 MeV) [Wikipedia – Neutron temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_temperature). But U-235 is far more likely to fission when struck by a **slow ("thermal") neutron** — a neutron in thermal equilibrium with the moderator at room temperature, ≈ **0.025 eV**, speed ≈ **2.2 km/s (2200 m/s)** [Wikipedia – Neutron temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_temperature); [Wikipedia – Neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator). The moderator's job is to slow the fast neutrons down to thermal energies *without* absorbing them, so they can sustain the chain reaction [IAEA – Nuclear Properties](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/graphiteknowledgebase/wiki/Wiki%20Pages/Nuclear%20Properties.aspx).

**The headline reduction:** a neutron goes from ~2 MeV / ~20,000 km/s down to ~0.025 eV / ~2.2 km/s — i.e. **energy reduced by a factor of ~8×10⁷ (≈80 million) and speed by a factor of ~10,000**.

## 2. Why light nuclei are effective (the derivable physics)

Moderation happens by **elastic collisions** between the neutron and the moderator nuclei [IAEA – Nuclear Properties](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/graphiteknowledgebase/wiki/Wiki%20Pages/Nuclear%20Properties.aspx). In a head-on elastic collision of a neutron (mass *m*) with a stationary nucleus (mass *M*), the **maximum fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy it can hand over** is

$$\frac{4mM}{(m+M)^2}$$

Taking *m* = 1 (neutron) and *M* = *A* (nucleus mass number):

| Moderator nucleus | A | Max energy lost in one head-on hit |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen (H) | 1 | 4·1/(2)² = **100%** — a head-on hit can stop the neutron |
| Deuterium (D) | 2 | 8/9 ≈ **89%** |
| Carbon (graphite) | 12 | 48/169 ≈ **28%** |
| Uranium-235 | 235 | ≈ **1.7%** |

This is the core reason **light nuclei are the best moderators**: the closer the target mass is to the neutron's mass, the more energy a single collision can remove. Heavy nuclei barely slow a neutron (they just "recoil" a little), which is why they make poor moderators. This is a clean, self-contained application of conservation of momentum + kinetic energy in elastic collisions — exactly the kind of result a Class 11 student can derive.

Because real collisions are rarely perfectly head-on, the *average* energy loss per collision is smaller, and it takes **many collisions** to thermalize a neutron. Standard textbook values (the average logarithmic energy decrement ξ, and the resulting number of collisions to reach thermal energy) are approximately:

| Moderator | ξ (avg. energy loss per collision) | ~Collisions to thermalize a ~MeV neutron |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen (H) | 1.0 | ~17–18 |
| Deuterium (D) | 0.725 | ~25–30 |
| Carbon (graphite) | 0.158 | ~90–115 |

So hydrogen is the most efficient *per collision* (fewest collisions), deuterium is a little less efficient, and graphite needs the most collisions. (These ξ and collision-count figures are standard reactor-physics values that follow from the elastic-collision physics above; the IAEA's discussion of "slowing-down power" and "moderating ratio" is the formal framework [IAEA – Nuclear Properties](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/graphiteknowledgebase/wiki/Wiki%20Pages/Nuclear%20Properties.aspx).)

## 3. The three common moderators and their real reactor context

A good moderator must do **two** things: (a) slow neutrons efficiently, and (b) **not absorb** them (absorption in anything but the fuel is "parasitic" and wastes neutrons) [IAEA – Nuclear Properties](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/graphiteknowledgebase/wiki/Wiki%20Pages/Nuclear%20Properties.aspx). The three common moderators trade off these two requirements:

- **Light water (H₂O) — hydrogen.** Hydrogen is the single best moderator (ξ = 1.0, fewest collisions), and water is cheap and dense. But ordinary hydrogen **absorbs a noticeable fraction of neutrons**, so a light-water reactor needs **enriched uranium** (typically ~3.5–5% U-235) to sustain the chain reaction. It is by far the most common: **~75% of the world's reactors** (PWRs and BWRs use water as both moderator and coolant) [Wikipedia – Neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator); [World Nuclear Association](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-power-reactors/overview/nuclear-power-reactors).

- **Heavy water (D₂O) — deuterium.** Deuterium is a slightly less efficient per-collision moderator (ξ = 0.725) but has a **much smaller neutron-absorption cross-section** than hydrogen, so it preserves neutrons. This lets a heavy-water reactor run on **natural (unenriched) uranium** (~0.7% U-235) — the defining feature of the Canadian **CANDU** reactor. About **~5% of reactors** [Wikipedia – Neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator); [World Nuclear Association](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-power-reactors/overview/nuclear-power-reactors).

- **Graphite (carbon, A = 12).** Carbon is the least efficient per collision (ξ = 0.158, needs ~90–115 collisions) but has **very low neutron absorption**, so it too can run on **natural uranium**. It is used in **~20% of reactors** (e.g. the Soviet/Russian **RBMK**, and the British **Magnox/AGR** gas-cooled reactors) [Wikipedia – Neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator); [World Nuclear Association](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-power-reactors/overview/nuclear-power-reactors).

**The key teaching contrast:** hydrogen is the *best* at slowing neutrons but *wastes* some by absorption (→ needs enrichment); deuterium and graphite are *worse* at slowing per collision but *waste almost none* (→ can use natural uranium). That trade-off is the whole reason three different moderators exist.

## 4. Tying it to "Work, Energy and Power"

- Each elastic collision is a **transfer of kinetic energy**: the neutron does work on the moderator nucleus, giving it kinetic energy (recoil), while total kinetic energy is conserved in the collision (non-relativistic). Over ~18 (H) to ~100+ (C) collisions the neutron's kinetic energy drops from ~2 MeV to ~0.025 eV.
- The energy the neutron loses ends up as **heat** in the moderator (the moderator is heated by the slowing-down process), which is then removed by the coolant — a direct link to energy conversion and heat transfer.
- The "100% vs 89% vs 28%" head-on numbers give students a concrete, calculable illustration of why mass ratio matters in collisions.

## 5. What is established vs. approximate

- **Established (from the fetched sources):** fission-neutron mean ≈ 2 MeV / ~20,000 km/s; thermal neutron ≈ 0.025 eV / ~2.2 km/s; moderator must slow *and* not absorb; light water ~75% / graphite ~20% / heavy water ~5%; light water needs enrichment while heavy water and graphite can use natural uranium.
- **Approximate / derived (present as such in class):** the per-collision energy-loss percentages (exact for head-on, from the 4A/(1+A)² formula) and the ξ values / collision counts (averages over all collision angles; order-of-magnitude). The exact collision count depends on the starting energy and the moderator, so quote it as "~18 for H, ~25–30 for D, ~90–115 for C."

**One caveat for accuracy:** the neutron-moderation example is *not* part of the NCERT Class 11 "Work, Energy and Power" chapter — it is a cross-disciplinary illustration you're adding. The physics (elastic collisions, energy transfer, conservation laws) is fully within the chapter's scope; the reactor specifics (enrichment, CANDU, RBMK) are extra context, so keep them as a short "real-world" box rather than exam content.
